questions.title: What constitutes a "pending or reasonably anticipated" enforcement proceeding under FOIA Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The court states that ongoing criminal investigations count as "proceedings" for purposes of Exemption 7(A), citing CREW. But I'm confused about the boundaries here. If an investigation has been ongoing for years (Farahi's case involved records from 2002 through at least 2023), at what point does it stop being "reasonably anticipated" that enforcement proceedings will actually occur? The court mentions that the investigation must be gathering evidence "for a possible future criminal case" - but is there any temporal limit? Can an agency just claim an investigation is indefinitely "ongoing" to permanently withhold records?

questions.title: How should courts evaluate supplemental declarations in FOIA cases - independently or in context of prior submissions?
questions.question_body: The court here says the Bender declaration shouldn't be considered "in isolation" because it was submitted only to "confirm that nothing had changed" since the earlier Hardy declaration. But Farahi argued that the Bender declaration was too conclusory on its face. When an agency submits an updated declaration years later, does it need to independently satisfy the government's burden, or can it rely on prior declarations to establish the underlying facts? How does a court determine whether an updated declaration is meant to 'establish from scratch' versus merely 'confirm' earlier showings?

questions.title: What makes nonexempt information "inextricably intertwined" with exempt information under FOIA's segregability requirement?
questions.question_body: The court rejects Farahi's segregability argument by saying that even if individual words could be disclosed, if exempt material is "interspersed line-by-line throughout the document," it's not "reasonably segregable." The court cites Mead Data for the proposition that FOIA is about "information, not simply words." I'm struggling with this distinction. If a document has some exempt facts and some nonexempt facts, how does a court decide whether the nonexempt facts constitute "information" that must be released versus mere "words" that can be withheld as intertwined? What practical standard do courts use?

questions.title: What role do ex parte declarations play in FOIA litigation, and can plaintiffs challenge the court's reliance on them?
questions.question_body: The court relied heavily on ex parte declarations here and acknowledges this "handicaps" FOIA plaintiffs, calling the problem "inherent" in cases where disclosure would defeat the exemption. But Farahi didn't oppose the acceptance of ex parte declarations, and the court says he therefore "cannot challenge" the court's reliance on them. Does failing to oppose the initial acceptance of ex parte submissions waive all later objections to how the court uses them? And practically speaking, how can a plaintiff ever successfully challenge ex parte evidence if they can't see what it says?

questions.title: How does deference to the FBI in national security cases interact with the government's burden of proof under FOIA?
questions.question_body: The court emphasizes "deference to the executive" in FOIA cases involving national security, citing CNSS. But it also says the FBI must "carry its burden" and show a "rational nexus" between the investigation and law enforcement duties. I'm confused about how deference and burden of proof work together. If the court defers to the FBI's characterization of records and its judgment about interference, isn't the government effectively relieved of its burden? What showing is the FBI actually required to make, and at what point does deference become de facto exemption from scrutiny?

questions.title: What level of specificity must agency declarations show under FOIA, and does it vary by issue?
questions.question_body: The court says the government may show the existence of enforcement proceedings simply by "attesting to their existence" (citing CREW), but also that declarations must show "reasonable specificity" why documents can't be segregated (citing Juarez). These seem like different standards. Does the required level of specificity differ depending on whether the issue is the existence of proceedings versus segregability? And for the "law enforcement purposes" prong, the court accepts a "rational nexus" test - is that a lower threshold than "reasonable specificity"?

questions.title: What showing must plaintiffs make to challenge an agency's categorical approach to FOIA withholding?
questions.question_body: The court says Farahi "forfeited" his argument about document categories because he provided "no specific explanation for why the various categories identified by the FBI were overbroad." But I thought the government bears the burden in FOIA cases. Does a plaintiff have the burden to specifically identify why each category is improper, or should the court independently evaluate whether categories are "sufficiently distinct"? What level of particularity must a plaintiff show to preserve a categorical challenge, and at what point in the litigation must this argument be made?
